The mathematics behind effectzones

Source: vignettes/articles/mathematics.Rmd
mathematics.Rmd

effectzones draws backgrounds; it never tests or classifies an estimate. But drawing a background still involves arithmetic: converting standardised thresholds to the scale of the data, choosing the right standard deviation, translating effect sizes into odds ratios, placing soft boundaries and fitting them into a panel. This article works through every one of those calculations.

Each calculator below starts from a concrete example. Press Next step to reveal one step at a time, Back to go back, or Show all. The numbers are computed by R with effectzones itself when this page is built, so they are exactly what the package uses.

1. The pooled within-group SD

Most effect-size benchmarks are standardised: a “medium” d of 0.5 means a difference of half a standard deviation. To draw it behind contrasts in the outcome’s own units we need that SD. In a one-way ANOVA with k groups the residual standard deviation is the pooled within-group SD,

s_p = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} (n_i - 1)\, s_i^2}{N - k}},

the usual denominator of Cohen’s d. It is the same quantity the ANOVA F test and the Tukey intervals rely on, under the same equal-variance assumption, so plot_contrasts() takes it from a one-way model automatically.

Pooled SD of the PlantGrowth one-way ANOVA
Given plant dry weight in three groups ( k = 3 ).
  1. Start from the size and SD of each group:
    group n_i s_i
    ctrl 10 0.5831
    trt1 10 0.7937
    trt2 10 0.4426
  2. Weight each group's variance by its degrees of freedom and add them up: the within-group sum of squares.
    \textstyle\sum (n_i - 1)s_i^2 = 9 \times 0.5831^2 + 9 \times 0.7937^2 + 9 \times 0.4426^2
    = 10.492
  3. Divide by the residual degrees of freedom to get the mean squared error.
    \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{10.492}{N - k} = \frac{10.492}{30 - 3} = 0.3886
  4. Take the square root: this is the pooled within-group SD.
    s_p = \sqrt{0.3886} = 0.6234
    It equals the residual SD of the fitted model, sigma(fit).
In R
fit <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
pooled_sd(fit)

2. From standardised thresholds to boundaries on the data scale

A standardised cut-point c becomes a pair of boundaries around the null, \text{null} \pm c \cdot \mathrm{SD}. Effect sizes on the correlation, \eta^2 or f scale are drawn on their own scale only; there is no conversion from them to raw differences.

Cohen's d benchmarks behind the PlantGrowth contrasts
Given cut-points d = 0.2,\ 0.5,\ 0.8 (Cohen 1988) and s_p = 0.6234 from calculator 1.
  1. Multiply each cut-point by the SD.
    0.2 \times 0.6234 = 0.1247,\quad 0.5 \times 0.6234 = 0.3117,\quad 0.8 \times 0.6234 = 0.4987
  2. Place a boundary on each side of the null (0 for a difference).
    \pm 0.1247,\quad \pm 0.3117,\quad \pm 0.4987
  3. Read off the zones (in kg of dry weight). A contrast whose interval lies between −0.1247 and 0.1247 kg sits in the negligible zone; beyond 0.4987 kg in either direction it reaches the large zone.
    \underbrace{|x| < 0.1247}_{\text{negligible}}\;\;\underbrace{0.1247 \le |x| < 0.3117}_{\text{small}}\;\;\underbrace{0.3117 \le |x| < 0.4987}_{\text{medium}}\;\;\underbrace{|x| \ge 0.4987}_{\text{large}}
In R
to_plot_scale(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), sd = pooled_sd(fit))

3. Which SD when the model has several terms

With more than one term the residual SD has the variance of every other term removed. That is right for factors the experimenter manipulated (their variation does not exist in the population) and too small for factors that were only measured (sex, age, site, baseline covariates), which are ordinary differences between people. The generalized standardizer (Olejnik & Algina 2003) keeps measured variation in the SD: refit the model with only the manipulated factors and use its residual SD. Whether a factor was manipulated or measured is a fact about the design, not the data, which is why plot_contrasts() asks instead of guessing.

Chilling (manipulated) and plant origin (measured) in the CO2 data
Given CO₂ uptake of 12 plants at the highest concentration; Treatment (chilled or not) was assigned, Type (Quebec or Mississippi) is the plants' origin.
  1. Fit the model with both terms. Its residual SD has the large difference between origins removed.
    s_{\text{residual}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{Treatment + Type}}} = 4.335 \quad (9\ \text{df})
  2. Refit with the manipulated factor only. Origin is ordinary variation between plants, so it goes back into the error term.
    s_{\text{gen}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}_{\text{Treatment}}} = 10.1 \quad (10\ \text{df})
  3. Compare. Using the residual SD would shrink every zone by this factor.
    \frac{s_{\text{gen}}}{s_{\text{residual}}} = \frac{10.1}{4.335} = 2.33
  4. Translate a "medium" d = 0.5 into each scale.
    0.5 \times 4.335 = 2.167 \ \mu\text{mol/m}^2\text{s} \quad\text{vs.}\quad 0.5 \times 10.1 = 5.048
    Only the second matches what "half a standard deviation between plants" means.
In R
fit <- aov(uptake ~ Treatment + Type, data = subset(CO2, conc == 1000))
plot_contrasts(fit, which = "Treatment",
  zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"),
                        sd = pooled_sd(update(fit, . ~ Treatment))))

The same logic applies to a randomised ANCOVA. Adjusting for a baseline covariate with pooled within-group correlation r removes a fraction r^2 of the outcome variance, so the adjusted residual SD relates to the unadjusted within-group SD approximately as

s_{\text{adj}} \approx s_{\text{unadj}} \sqrt{1 - r^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s_{\text{unadj}} \approx \frac{s_{\text{adj}}}{\sqrt{1 - r^2}},

(ignoring the one degree of freedom spent on the slope). The standardizer for d is s_{\text{unadj}}: the covariate improves precision, but people still differ by that much.

4. The SD is an estimate too

The SD used to place the boundaries has sampling error. Under normality, (\nu\, s^2)/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_\nu with \nu residual degrees of freedom, which gives a confidence interval for \sigma:

\left[\, s\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\chi^2_{\nu,\,1-\alpha/2}}},\; s\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\chi^2_{\nu,\,\alpha/2}}} \,\right].

Each boundary d \cdot s inherits that interval. effectzones does not yet draw this uncertainty, so report it alongside the plot.

95% confidence interval for the PlantGrowth SD
Given s_p = 0.6234 with \nu = 27 residual degrees of freedom (calculator 1).
  1. Look up the chi-square quantiles that cut off 2.5% in each tail.
    \chi^2_{27,\,0.975} = 43.19, \qquad \chi^2_{27,\,0.025} = 14.57
  2. Lower limit: divide by the larger quantile.
    0.6234 \sqrt{\tfrac{27}{43.19}} = 0.4929
  3. Upper limit: divide by the smaller quantile.
    0.6234 \sqrt{\tfrac{27}{14.57}} = 0.8485
  4. Carry it to a boundary. The "medium" boundary 0.5 SD could plausibly lie anywhere in
    0.5 \times [0.4929,\ 0.8485] = [0.2464,\ 0.4242]\ \text{kg}
    A point boundary at 0.3117 kg hides that spread.
In R
s <- pooled_sd(fit); nu <- fit$df.residual
s * sqrt(nu / qchisq(c(0.975, 0.025), nu))

5. Soft boundaries

Benchmarks are conventions, not natural discontinuities, so by default geom_es_zones() fades from one zone into the next. For a boundary at distance c from the null, with softness = \lambda (default 0.1), the transition spans

\left[\, c - \tfrac{\lambda c}{2},\; c + \tfrac{\lambda c}{2} \,\right],

drawn as n thin rectangles (n_slices, default 40). Slice j is coloured at the fraction t_j = (j - \tfrac12)/n of the way between the two zone colours, interpolated in the perceptually uniform CIELAB space. If two neighbouring transitions would overlap they are both cut back to the midpoint between their boundaries. For ratio zones the same arithmetic is done on the log scale.

The soft boundary between "small" and "medium" (PlantGrowth, d = 0.5)
Given c = 0.5 \times 0.6234 = 0.3117 kg, \lambda = 0.1 , n = 40 slices, grey palette.
  1. Width of the transition: a tenth of the threshold.
    \lambda c = 0.1 \times 0.3117 = 0.03117
  2. Centre it on the threshold.
    [\,0.3117 - 0.01558,\; 0.3117 + 0.01558\,] = [\,0.2961,\; 0.3273\,]
  3. Cut it into 40 slices and give each one a mixing fraction, e.g. slices 1, 20 and 40:
    t_1 = \tfrac{0.5}{40} = 0.0125,\quad t_{20} = \tfrac{19.5}{40} = 0.4875,\quad t_{40} = \tfrac{39.5}{40} = 0.9875
  4. Mix the two zone colours (#BBBBBB small, #7A7A7A medium) at those fractions in CIELAB:
    slice 1#BABABA   slice 20#9B9B9B   slice 40#7B7B7B
    Each slice is then drawn with the layer's alpha (0.35 by default), so the gridlines and estimates stay visible.
In R
geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), sd = pooled_sd(fit),
              softness = 0.1, n_slices = 40)

6. Ratios: zones on the log scale

Odds ratios and risk ratios are multiplicative, so their zones are placed around 1 on the log scale. A magnitude c gives boundaries 1/c and c (symmetric in \log), unless the thresholds specify a different magnitude below the null (cuts_lower). On a scale_x_log10() axis, ggplot2 works in \log_{10} units, and the boundaries are transformed the same way as the data.

Placing the first Chen et al. odds-ratio boundary on a log axis
Given c = 1.68 (the "small" odds ratio at a 1% baseline risk), null = 1 , axis \log_{10} .
  1. Above the null: multiply.
    1 \times 1.68 = 1.68
  2. Below the null (symmetric case): divide.
    1 / 1.68 = 0.5952
  3. On the log scale the two are mirror images of each other.
    \log(1.68) = 0.5188, \qquad \log(0.5952) = -0.5188
  4. ggplot2 places them at their log10 positions, exactly like the data.
    \log_{10}(0.5952) = -0.2253, \qquad \log_{10}(1.68) = 0.2253
    Section 8 shows why, under Chen et al.'s own model, the lower boundary is not exactly 1/c.
In R
geom_es_zones(es_thresholds(c(1.68, 3.47, 6.71), c("negligible", "small", "medium", "large"),
                            metric = "or"), scale = "log", null = 1) +
  scale_x_log10()

7. From d to an odds ratio: Chinn’s approximation

If a binary outcome arises from dichotomising a latent variable with a logistic distribution, a shift of d standard deviations corresponds to

\log(\mathrm{OR}) = d \cdot \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 1.814\, d

(Chinn 2000). This is what to_plot_scale(…, scale = "log") uses for d thresholds. It does not depend on the baseline risk, which is exactly where it differs from Chen et al.

A "medium" d = 0.5 as an odds ratio (Chinn 2000)
Given d = 0.5
  1. The scale factor of the logistic distribution.
    \pi/\sqrt{3} = 1.8138
  2. Multiply.
    \log(\mathrm{OR}) = 0.5 \times 1.8138 = 0.9069
  3. Exponentiate.
    \mathrm{OR} = e^{0.9069} = 2.477
    Compare Chen et al. at a 1% baseline: 3.47 (next section).
In R
to_plot_scale(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), scale = "log")$cuts

8. From d to an odds ratio at a given baseline risk: Chen et al.

Chen, Cohen & Chen (2010) place both groups on a latent normal scale. With event risk p_0 in the reference group, a shift d gives the exposed group’s risk and the odds ratio

p_1 = \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(p_0) + d\right), \qquad \mathrm{OR} = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_0/(1-p_0)} .

This reproduces their published values (1.68, 3.47 and 6.71 at p_0 = 1\%; 1.52, 2.74 and 4.72 at 5\%). Applied to a protective shift -d it does not give 1/\mathrm{OR}, except at p_0 = 0.5, so effectzones computes the boundaries below 1 from -d directly.

The "large" boundaries (d = ±0.8) at a 1% baseline risk
Given p_0 = 0.01 in the reference group, d = 0.8 .
  1. Move the baseline risk to the latent normal scale.
    z_0 = \Phi^{-1}(0.01) = -2.3263
  2. Harmful direction: shift by +d and return to a risk.
    p_1 = \Phi(-2.3263 + 0.8) = \Phi(-1.5263) = 0.06346
  3. Odds ratio for the harmful direction (the published value, 6.71).
    \mathrm{OR} = \frac{0.06346/(1-0.06346)}{0.01/0.99} = 6.708
  4. Protective direction: shift by −d instead.
    p_1 = \Phi(-2.3263 - 0.8) = \Phi(-3.1263) = 0.000885
  5. Odds ratio for the protective direction.
    \mathrm{OR} = \frac{0.000885/(1-0.000885)}{0.01/0.99} = 0.08769 = 1/11.4
    Mirroring would have put this boundary at 1/6.708 = 0.1491, so the protective "large" zone would start too close to 1.
In R
chen_or_thresholds(0.01)   # any baseline risk: chen_or_thresholds(0.2)

9. Distribution-based (provisional) MCIDs

A distribution-based MCID describes the spread or the measurement error of a score, not what patients consider worthwhile, so effectzones marks it provisional. Two rules are offered:

\text{half SD} = 0.5\, s, \qquad \text{SEM} = s\sqrt{1 - r_{xx}},

where r_{xx} is the instrument’s reliability (Norman, Sloan & Wyrwich 2003; Wyrwich, Tierney & Wolinsky 1999). Half an SD is exactly Cohen’s “medium” d = 0.5, which is why a distribution-based MCID adds no clinical information beyond the effect-size zones.

Half-SD and SEM for a score with SD 10 and reliability 0.84
Given s = 10 , r_{xx} = 0.84 .
  1. Half an SD.
    0.5 \times 10 = 5
  2. The unreliable fraction of the variance.
    1 - 0.84 = 0.16
  3. One standard error of measurement.
    10 \times \sqrt{0.16} = 10 \times 0.4 = 4
  4. Either value becomes a symmetric, provisional MCID.
    \text{harm} < -4 \le \text{trivial} \le 4 < \text{benefit}
    The legend then reads "MCID (provisional, distribution-based)".
In R
mcid_distribution(sd = 10, method = "sem", reliability = 0.84)

10. MCID zones: asymmetry, direction, ranges and multiples

An MCID defines a trivial zone [\ell, u] around the null, with \ell < 0 < u allowed to differ in size. Which side is benefit depends on direction. A range for either threshold (an uncertain MCID) is drawn as a fade across the range, using the same slicing as section 5. With beyond = "multiples", extra boundaries at 2\ell, 3\ell and 2u, 3u deepen the colour; this requires point thresholds, because multiples of an uncertain MCID would be uncertain too.

Zones for an asymmetric MCID (−0.25 / +0.3, higher is better)
Given \ell = -0.25 , u = 0.3 , direction = "higher_better".
  1. Three zones, with hard edges at the thresholds.
    \underbrace{x < -0.25}_{\text{harm}} \quad \underbrace{-0.25 \le x \le 0.3}_{\text{trivial}} \quad \underbrace{x > 0.3}_{\text{benefit}}
  2. If lower values were better (direction = "lower_better"), the same boundaries would label the sides the other way round.
    \underbrace{x < -0.25}_{\text{benefit}} \quad \underbrace{-0.25 \le x \le 0.3}_{\text{trivial}} \quad \underbrace{x > 0.3}_{\text{harm}}
  3. With beyond = "multiples", add boundaries at 2 and 3 times each threshold.
    -0.75,\ -0.5,\ -0.25,\ 0.3,\ 0.6,\ 0.9
  4. If the improvement threshold were uncertain, say between 0.3 and 0.5, the trivial zone fades into benefit across that range instead of switching at one point.
    0.3 \le x \le 0.5:\ \text{trivial} \rightarrow \text{benefit}
    Multiples are then refused: "2×" could be anywhere from 0.6 to 1.0.
In R
geom_mcid_zones(mcid_thresholds(lower = -0.25, upper = 0.3), beyond = "multiples")
geom_mcid_zones(mcid_thresholds(lower = -0.25, upper = c(0.3, 0.5)))

11. Where the intervals come from: Tukey’s HSD

effectzones does not compute intervals; plot_contrasts() draws the ones your analysis produced. For Tukey post-hoc comparisons (computed by stats::TukeyHSD()), the family-wise interval for groups i and j is

(\bar y_i - \bar y_j) \pm \frac{q_{1-\alpha;\,k,\,\nu}}{\sqrt 2} \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}\left(\frac{1}{n_i} + \frac{1}{n_j}\right)},

where q is a quantile of the studentized range distribution.

The trt2 − trt1 interval in PlantGrowth
Given \bar y_{\text{trt2}} = 5.526,\ \bar y_{\text{trt1}} = 4.661 , n = 10 per group, \mathrm{MSE} = 0.3886 , k = 3,\ \nu = 27 .
  1. Difference in means.
    5.526 - 4.661 = 0.865
  2. Studentized range quantile for 95% family-wise coverage.
    q_{0.95;\,3,\,27} = 3.506
  3. Half-width of the interval.
    \frac{3.506}{\sqrt 2}\sqrt{0.3886\left(\tfrac{1}{10} + \tfrac{1}{10}\right)} = 0.6912
  4. The interval drawn by plot_contrasts(), identical to TukeyHSD().
    0.865 \pm 0.6912 = [\,0.1738,\ 1.556\,]
    Against the d zones of calculator 2 (boundaries at ±0.1247, ±0.3117, ±0.4987 kg), this interval runs from the small zone into the large zone.
In R
plot_contrasts(fit, zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d")))

12. Fitting zones into the panel

Zone boundaries are layer parameters, not data, so by default they never change the axis limits. The layer works out what is visible in three steps: transform the boundaries like the data, keep the zones that reach the visible range, and clip them to the panel. The visible range is the data range expanded by ggplot2’s default 5% on each side. (Zooming with coord_cartesian() is applied only at drawing time, so the legend can still list a zone that the zoom cuts away.)

Which Cohen's d zones appear in the PlantGrowth Tukey plot
Given the three Tukey intervals and the boundaries from calculator 2.
  1. The data span the lowest and highest interval limits.
    [\,-1.062,\ 1.556\,]
  2. Expand by 5% of the width on each side to get the visible range.
    [\,-1.062 - 0.1309,\ 1.556 + 0.1309\,] = [\,-1.193,\ 1.687\,]
  3. Keep a zone if it overlaps the visible range: its upper end is above the left edge and its lower end below the right edge.
    \text{keep} \iff \text{hi} > \text{left} \ \text{and}\ \text{lo} < \text{right}
  4. Result: ✔ large, ✔ medium, ✔ small, ✔ negligible, ✔ small, ✔ medium, ✔ large. Every zone reaches the visible range, so all four labels appear in the legend; the outermost ones are clipped at the panel edges.
  5. Now suppose the benchmark's SD were 3 kg. The boundaries move to ±0.6, ±1.5, ±2.4 kg. Result: ✘ large, ✘ medium, ✔ small, ✔ negligible, ✔ small, ✔ medium, ✘ large. The large zones begin beyond the visible range on both sides, so large is left out of the legend.
In R
plot_contrasts(fit, zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"))) # expand = FALSE
plot_contrasts(fit, zones = geom_es_zones(es_benchmarks("cohen_d"), expand = TRUE))

With expand = TRUE the finite boundaries are added to the scale’s range instead, so every cut-point is visible and every zone is listed.

References

Chen H, Cohen P, Chen S (2010). How big is a big odds ratio? Interpreting the magnitudes of odds ratios in epidemiological studies. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation 39(4):860-864. doi:10.1080/03610911003650383

Chinn S (2000). A simple method for converting an odds ratio to effect size for use in meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine 19(22):3127-3131. doi:10.1002/1097-0258(20001130)19:22<3127::AID-SIM784>3.0.CO;2-M

Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum. doi:10.4324/9780203771587

Norman GR, Sloan JA, Wyrwich KW (2003). Interpretation of changes in health-related quality of life: the remarkable universality of half a standard deviation. Medical Care 41(5):582-592. doi:10.1097/01.mlr.0000062554.74615.4c

Olejnik S, Algina J (2003). Generalized eta and omega squared statistics: measures of effect size for some common research designs. Psychological Methods 8(4):434-447. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.4.434

Wyrwich KW, Tierney WM, Wolinsky FD (1999). Further evidence supporting an SEM-based criterion for identifying meaningful intra-individual changes in health-related quality of life. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 52(9):861-873. doi:10.1016/s0895-4356(99)00071-2
